title: An experimental design and implementation protocol for testing a dashboard for improving sustainable healthy food choice
author: de la Fuente, Kwofie, et al.
materials: Testing of McGill DISH through the web or mobile application: Participants' food choices in the cafeterias were monitored throughout the ten weeks. In the first five weeks, all participants used the pseudo-McGill DISH application for meal purchases. After this period, participants in the treatment group purchased food using the McGill DISH, while the control group continued to use the pseudo-McGill DISH application for meal ordering for five weeks. The application was accessible on smartphones, tablets, or any smart device. The participants in the treatment group were exposed to the environmental and nutritional indicators associated with each meal. Other relevant features, such as meal comparison and resource page, were visible for the treatment group (See the reference for the tested application [5]). At the same time, the contrary was done for the control group, who were exposed to the pseudo-McGill DISH. This provided an excellent opportunity to compare participants' dietary choices with and without introducing sustainability information, shedding light on any shifts in their meal preferences and selections. Furthermore, each participant purchased at least one meal a week at the participating cafeteria over a ten-week trial period. At the end of the tenth-week trial period, participants in the treatment group were requested to complete a DISH concept questionnaire to gauge their clarity regarding the terminologies used on the software and how they subsequently influence their choices during meal purchases.

Fig. 4 outlines the primary purpose of each questionnaire and the feedback provided, along with the methods, tools, and software used for statistical analysis. Descriptive statistical analysis will be calculated using the mean and standard deviation for the sociodemographic data and purchasing records from the trial sessions. A cross-tabulation analysis and analysis of variance will be used to examine the relationship and influence of demographic and purchase motivation variables on consumption frequency responses and meal purchases through the McGill DISH application. A baseline characteristic between the control and treatment groups will be compared using an analysis of variance, the Kruskal-Wallis test, and the Chi-square test, depending on the variable type. The significance level will be set at a p-value <0.05. Furthermore, we will employ latent profile analysis (LPA) to explore subgroups of participants who display similar patterns of multiple motivations for multiple consumers and to examine differences in subjective purchases across these subtypes [18,19].Fig. 4Characteristics of data, statistical analysis, and tools/software for the respective analysis.Fig 4:

The LPA works on the assumption that sample (residual) variance can be reduced by assuming a categorical latent variable that effectively subdivides the sample into ≥2 subgroups that are more homogeneous in terms of their patterns of variable means and (co)variance. Fortunately, ongoing development in the scientific field now allows LPA to be conducted in an open-source R-platform. Furthermore, odds ratios and a 95 % confidence interval will be calculated to measure the likelihood of choosing the meal with the most favorable score for the treatment group compared to the control group. These analyses will be done using MATLAB and Python statistical packages in combination with Microsoft Excel and the Statistical Package for Social Sciences software (SPSS by IBM Corp). The obtained analyzed data will be visualized using R-library ggplot2, Python-Seaborn and Matplotlib, and MATLAB data visualization packages.

steps.title: Define eligibility and recruit participants
steps.instruction: Establish eligibility criteria, prepare recruitment materials, and invite eligible individuals to join the study.

steps.title: Obtain consent and baseline data
steps.instruction: Have each participant complete a 2‑minute survey, sign a consent form, and fill out a sociodemographic background questionnaire before proceeding.

steps.title: Assign pseudo‑identifications
steps.instruction: Generate a unique pseudo‑user ID for each participant (e.g., DISH‑XA01) and record it so that names remain encoded during the study.

steps.title: Administer initial questionnaires
steps.instruction: Provide participants with a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) and a meal decision questionnaire; after submission, email an infographic that explains how to install and log into the pseudo‑McGill DISH application.

substeps.instruction: Include instructions for accessing the pseudo version via website or mobile app.
Explain that the pseudo version lacks environmental and nutritional indicators.

steps.title: Baseline app usage (Weeks 1‑5)
steps.instruction: Instruct all participants to use the pseudo‑McGill DISH for meal purchases for five consecutive weeks, making at least one cafeteria purchase per week.

substeps.instruction: Compensate participants CAD 7 each week based on their purchase history.

steps.title: Randomize into treatment and control groups
steps.instruction: After the five‑week baseline, randomly assign participants to either the treatment group or the control group.

steps.title: Provide treatment group orientation
steps.instruction: Give treatment participants information on the primary purpose of DISH, its features, scoring metrics, and the meaning of environmental and nutritional scores.

substeps.instruction: Explain environmental and dietary scales for individuals and average scores for selected meals.

steps.title: App usage post‑randomization (Weeks 6‑8)
steps.instruction: Continue app usage for three weeks: treatment participants use the authentic McGill DISH (displaying all indicators), while control participants keep using the pseudo version.

substeps.instruction: During this period, treatment participants review their previous environmental and nutritional scores.
Both groups complete the DISH concepts questionnaire and the Environmental/Nutritional questionnaire at the end of the three weeks.

steps.title: Complete remaining study period (Weeks 9‑10)
steps.instruction: All participants keep using their assigned app version (authentic for treatment, pseudo for control) for the final two weeks, ensuring at least one meal purchase per week.

steps.title: Final questionnaire and feedback (Week 10)
steps.instruction: At the end of the tenth week, provide participants with updated environmental and nutritional scores and administer the same questionnaire used in week 5, plus a feedback questionnaire on the DISH application across web, mobile, and kiosk platforms.

substeps.instruction: Compensate each participant a total of CAD 70 for the entire study.
Enter participants who completed all meals and questionnaires into a draw for a CAD 100 gift card.

steps.title: Deploy DISH self‑service kiosk (Weeks 11‑12)
steps.instruction: Install the DISH kiosk in participating cafeterias for a two‑week period; participants use the kiosk version that matches their group (pseudo for control, authentic for treatment) based on their pseudo‑ID.

substeps.instruction: After kiosk use, have all participants complete a DISH concept questionnaire and a feedback questionnaire.

steps.title: Statistical analysis of study data
steps.instruction: Analyze collected data using the following methods and software:

substeps.instruction: Calculate descriptive statistics (mean, standard deviation) for sociodemographic data and purchase records.
Perform cross‑tabulation, ANOVA, Kruskal‑Wallis, and Chi‑square tests to examine relationships between demographics, motivations, and meal purchases.
Compare baseline characteristics between groups using ANOVA, Kruskal‑Wallis, or Chi‑square as appropriate; set significance at p < 0.05.
Conduct latent profile analysis (LPA) in R to identify ≥2 homogeneous subgroups.
Compute odds ratios and 95 % confidence intervals for the likelihood of choosing high‑score meals (treatment vs. control) using MATLAB, Python, and SPSS.
Visualize results with R‑library ggplot2, Python‑Seaborn, Python‑Matplotlib, and MATLAB visualization tools.
